claim: Recent advances in fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using Oligopaint probes have enabled super-resolution imaging of genomic domains with a resolution limit of 4.9 kb.
source: Recent advances in fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using Oligopaint probes have enabled super-resolution imaging of genomic domains with a resolution limit of 4.9 kb.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on Oligopaint-FISH methods.

claim: The authors developed a FISH method using molecular beacon (MB) probes to facilitate probe-target binding while minimizing non-specific fluorescence.
source: To target shorter elements, we developed a simple FISH method that uses molecular beacon (MB) probes to facilitate the probe-target binding, while minimizing non-specific fluorescence.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the method development described in the manuscript.

claim: Using 3D-STORM with optimized imaging conditions, the authors efficiently distinguished sparsely distributed Alexa-647 from background cellular autofluorescence.
source: We used three-dimensional stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (3D-STORM) with optimized imaging conditions to efficiently distinguish sparsely distributed Alexa-647 from background cellular autofluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing optimization of imaging conditions.

claim: Utilizing 3D-STORM and only 29–34 individual MB probes, the authors observed 3D fine-scale nanostructures of 2.5 kb integrated or endogenous unique DNA in situ in human or mouse genome, respectively.
source: Utilizing 3D-STORM and only 29–34 individual MB probes, we observed 3D fine-scale nanostructures of 2.5 kb integrated or endogenous unique DNA in situ in human or mouse genome, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and images.

claim: The MB-based FISH method is capable of visualizing the shortest non-repetitive genomic sequence in 3D at super-resolution reported to date.
source: We demonstrated our MB-based FISH method was capable of visualizing the so far shortest non-repetitive genomic sequence in 3D at super-resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior methods and experimental demonstration.

claim: Chromosome conformation capture (3C)-based methods can only reveal three-dimensional (3D) chromatin interactions as the cell population average.
source: Being able to visualize short unique genomic sequences in situ at high resolution is essential to understanding looping interactions and chromatin organization in single cells, but chromosome conformation capture (3C)-based methods can only reveal three-dimensional (3D) chromatin interactions as the cell population average (Guo et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2015; Dixon et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016; Dekker and Misteli, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on 3C-based methods.

claim: Oligopaint probe-based FISH combined with STORM enables super-resolution visualization of genomic domains at a sequence resolution limit of 4.9 kb.
source: A recent study combined oligopaint probe-based FISH (Oligopaint-FISH) with stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM) to enable super-resolution visualization of genomic domains at a sequence resolution limit of 4.9 kb (Boettiger et al., 2016; Beliveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: STORM is a high-resolution single-molecule imaging technique that relies on the stochastic activation and localization of many individual photo-switchable fluorescent dyes.
source: STORM is a high-resolution single-molecule imaging technique, which relies on the stochastic activation and localization of many individual photo-switchable fluorescent dyes (Bates et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on STORM.

claim: Targeting a genomic region with Oligopaints requires hundreds to thousands of probes derived using a complicated probe generation system.
source: Targeting a genomic region requires hundreds to thousands of Oligopaints that are derived using a complicated probe generation system.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of Oligopaint methodology from prior literature.

claim: High-resolution imaging of Oligopaint-labeled targets requires a secondary probe and the pairing of fluorophores on both probes to achieve sufficient numbers of localizations.
source: Furthermore, high-resolution imaging of Oligopaint-labeled targets requires a secondary probe and the pairing of fluorophores on both probes to achieve sufficient numbers of localizations needed to resolve fine-scale nanostructures (Thompson et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2010; Deschout et al., 2014; Beliveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Oligopaint-FISH.

claim: Short genomic elements have been shown to play many essential roles in genomic functions.
source: Short genomic elements have been shown to play many essential roles in genomic functions (Blinka et al., 2016; Hogan et al., 2015), but high-resolution visualization of elements smaller than the resolution limit of the above method is currently not possible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: High-resolution visualization of genomic elements smaller than 4.9 kb was not possible with existing methods prior to this work.
source: Short genomic elements have been shown to play many essential roles in genomic functions (Blinka et al., 2016; Hogan et al., 2015), but high-resolution visualization of elements smaller than the resolution limit of the above method is currently not possible.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with prior methods and their limitations.

claim: Molecular beacon probes carry a fluorescent dye and quencher at separate ends and assume a hairpin configuration that turns off fluorescence when not bound to the target sequence.
source: To decrease non-specific fluorescence, we designed FISH probes in the form of molecular beacons that carry a fluorescent dye and quencher at separate ends. When not bound to the target sequence, these probes assume a hairpin configuration that turns off the fluorescence (Tyagi and Kramer, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on molecular beacons and the design described in the manuscript.

claim: Alexa-647 was chosen as the fluorescent dye due to its well-documented ability to switch between dark and fluorescent states when used in STORM imaging.
source: Alexa-647 was chosen as the fluorescent dye due to its well-documented ability to switch between dark and fluorescent states when used in STORM imaging (Dempsey et al., 2011; Heilemann et al., 2009; Olivier et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Alexa-647 properties.

claim: Black hole quencher 3 (BHQ3) is a specific quencher for Alexa-647.
source: Black hole quencher 3 (BHQ3, a specific quencher for Alexa-647) (Didenko, 2001), was tethered to the other end of probe to quench the fluorescence of the MB when unbound or non-specifically associated, which ensures the MB probe fluoresces only upon binding with its target (Figure 1a, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on BHQ3.

claim: The MB probe fluoresces only upon binding with its target.
source: Black hole quencher 3 (BHQ3, a specific quencher for Alexa-647) (Didenko, 2001), was tethered to the other end of probe to quench the fluorescence of the MB when unbound or non-specifically associated, which ensures the MB probe fluoresces only upon binding with its target (Figure 1a, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by the design principle and Figure 1a showing the mechanism.

claim: A 3.3 kb non-repetitive lentiviral region was randomly inserted into the human genome by viral infection.
source: A 3.3 kb non-repetitive lentiviral region (blue) between 5' and 3' LTRs was randomly inserted into the human genome by viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The target DNA was a 2.5 kb sequence containing a CMV promoter and an egfp gene within the 3.3 kb inserted region.
source: The target DNA was a 2.5 kb sequence containing a CMV promoter and an egfp gene within the 3.3 kb inserted region, which was then labeled with the 29 specific MB probes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 29 specific MB probes were designed to label the 2.5 kb target sequence in the integrated viral DNA.
source: The target DNA was a 2.5 kb sequence containing a CMV promoter and an egfp gene within the 3.3 kb inserted region, which was then labeled with the 29 specific MB probes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and Figure 1b.

claim: PCR confirmed the integration of lentiviral DNA in EGFP cells.
source: PCR confirmation of lentiviral integration in the human genome. Using primers targeting the 3.3 kb inserted lentiviral regions (lanes 1–4), a 3.3 kb electrophoretic band was amplified from the lentiviral plasmid (lane 4) and genomic DNA of EGFP cells (lane 2), but not from blank controls (lane 1) or PCR mixture without any template (lane 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Most sorted EGFP cells (92.9 ± 1.5%) remained fluorescent green after eight further culture passages.
source: Most of these sorted cells (92.9 ± 1.5%; right peak, solid line) remained fluorescent green after eight further culture passages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No tandem repeats of viral DNA were detected in a single inserted locus in EGFP cells.
source: No larger bands of multiples of 3.3 kb were observed in EGFP cell samples (lane 2), indicating no tandem repeats in a single inserted locus. It was also confirmed by an additional PCR test (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Each MB probe contained a 42-nucleotide (nt) hybridizing region for specific binding to sites along the target strand, as well as two flanking 7-nt arm regions that formed the hairpin structure.
source: Each MB probe contained a 42-nucleotide (nt) hybridizing region for specific binding to sites along the target strand, as well as two flanking 7-nt arm regions that formed the hairpin structure (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim describes the design of MB probes used in the study.

claim: Individual MB probes showed high fluorescence intensity in the presence of corresponding complementary sequences (CS) but low fluorescence (19.0 ± 7.1%) in the presence of non-complementary sequences (NCSs).
source: The spectrophotometry analysis showed high fluorescence intensity for MB probes in the presence of corresponding CS (gray bars), but low fluorescence (19.0 ± 7.1% when normalized to that from CS group) in the presence of NCSs (black bars, Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectrophotometry data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Each unbound/non-specifically associated MB probe had low potential fluorescence of less than a quarter even in the presence of excessive amounts of NCSs sharing 10 ± 5 nt complementarity.
source: This data suggested each unbound/non-specifically associated MB probe had low potential fluorescence of less than a quarter even in the presence of excessive amounts of NCSs sharing 10 ± 5 nt complementarity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the spectrophotometry data in Figure 1d.

claim: The hybridization step of oligonucleotide probes in FISH has usually been performed at a relatively high temperature (ranging from 37°C to 47°C) to diminish off-target binding.
source: To diminish off-target binding when labeling a unique target, the hybridization step of the oligonucleotide probes in FISH has usually been performed at a relatively high temperature (ranging from 37°C to 47°C) (Beliveau et al., 2015, 2012; Yamada et al., 2011; Boyle et al., 2011; Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior FISH methods.

claim: When the hybridization temperature decreased from 42°C to 14°C, MB-CS binding increased.
source: As expected, when the hybridization temperature decreased from 42°C to 14°C, MB-CS binding increased (Figure 1e, solid line with circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectrophotometry data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The binding of MBs to NCSs gradually diminished with lower temperature, probably due to the hairpin structure of the probe preventing it from associating with NCSs.
source: Surprisingly, the binding of MBs to NCSs gradually diminished with lower temperature (dashed lines with triangles), probably due to the hairpin structure of the probe preventing it from associating with NCSs.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectrophotometry data shown in Figure 1e and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The optimal temperature range for MB binding to its single stranded target site was 22°C to 14°C.
source: Our results suggested the optimal temperature range for MB binding to its single stranded target site was 22°C to 14°C, which was used to determine the final temperature for MB hybridization.
evidence: This claim is based on the temperature-dependent binding data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Oligopaint-FISH requires an Alexa-405 activator to pair and assist the Cy5 to ensure detection of the fine-scale nanostructure of Cy5-labeled DNA.
source: Because a non-repetitive genomic sequence is labeled at a much lower density than a repetitive sequence, Oligopaint-FISH requires an Alexa-405 activator to pair and assist the Cy5 to ensure detection of the fine-scale nanostructure of Cy5-labeled DNA (Boettiger et al., 2016; Beliveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior Oligopaint-FISH methods.

claim: Sparsely distributed Alexa-647 could be efficiently distinguished from the cellular background even in the absence of an activator dye by optimizing the conditions of STORM imaging.
source: Our recent work suggested that sparsely distributed Alexa-647 could be efficiently distinguished from the cellular background even in the absence of an activator dye by optimizing the conditions of STORM imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimization experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The lowest false discovery rate (FDR) was observed from condition XII (85 Hz, 18 W/cm2 405 nm laser and 1 kW/cm2 641 nm laser).
source: Although various laser power densities and frame rates have been used in other studies (Doksani et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2008b; Olivier et al., 2013; Rust et al., 2006; van de Linde et al., 2011), we observed the lowest FDR from condition XII (85 Hz, 18 W/cm2 405 nm laser and 1 kW/cm2641 nm laser; marked with asterisk in Figure 2b), which was the optimal condition for imaging sparsely distributed Alexa-647.
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Condition XII was the optimal condition for imaging sparsely distributed Alexa-647.
source: Although various laser power densities and frame rates have been used in other studies (Doksani et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2008b; Olivier et al., 2013; Rust et al., 2006; van de Linde et al., 2011), we observed the lowest FDR from condition XII (85 Hz, 18 W/cm2 405 nm laser and 1 kW/cm2641 nm laser; marked with asterisk in Figure 2b), which was the optimal condition for imaging sparsely distributed Alexa-647.
evidence: This claim is supported by optimization data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Condition XII still had the lowest FDR among all analyzed conditions in a modified imaging buffer at pH 7.5 with reduced glucose oxidase and catalase concentrations.
source: In this non-ideal imaging environment, condition XII still had the lowest FDR among all analyzed conditions (Figure 2c), indicating it was the most optimal condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by FDR data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The highest proportion of events during the whole imaging process occurred under the optimized condition (XII) compared to other conditions.
source: The highest proportion of events during the whole imaging process still occurred under the optimized condition (dark line) compared to the other conditions (Figure 2d, colored lines), indicating less photo-bleaching of Alexa-647 in optimized condition XII.
evidence: This claim is supported by photo-bleaching data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In cells with extremely sparse distributions of Alexa-647 (input concentration of 80 pM), fluorescence signals could be efficiently identified only under optimized conditions.
source: In cells with extremely sparse distributions of Alexa-647 (input concentration of 80 pM), fluorescence signals could be efficiently identified only under optimized conditions, likely due to differences in autofluorescence of the control samples between unoptimized and optimized conditions (3.15 ± 0.17 vs. 0.12 ± 0.05 events per µm2; Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by detection efficiency data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The optimized condition was more suitable for very sparsely labeled cases.
source: This indicated the optimized condition was more suitable for very sparsely labeled cases, although conditions comparable to the unoptimized conditions could work in densely labeled targets (Huang et al., 2008a, 2008b).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of detection efficiency data and includes citations to prior work.

claim: More switching events were observed using the optimized conditions compared to unoptimized conditions in samples with relatively high Alexa-647 density.
source: In samples with relatively high Alexa-647 density (input concentration of 200 pM or 2 nM), we observed more switching events using the optimized conditions (gray bars) compared to unoptimized conditions (white bars) after subtracting the corresponding autofluorescence events (Figure 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by event detection data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The standard deviations of the distribution of localizations from Alexa-647 were 9 nm in lateral and 22 nm in axial dimensions.
source: The standard deviations of the distribution of these localizations were 9 nm in lateral and 22 nm in axial dimensions, and the corresponding full width at half maximum (FWHM) values were 22 nm and 52 nm, respectively (Figure 3b), which yielded a resolution of 20–30 nm in x-y and 50–60 nm in z directions.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization precision data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The corresponding full width at half maximum (FWHM) values were 22 nm and 52 nm in lateral and axial dimensions, respectively.
source: The standard deviations of the distribution of these localizations were 9 nm in lateral and 22 nm in axial dimensions, and the corresponding full width at half maximum (FWHM) values were 22 nm and 52 nm, respectively (Figure 3b), which yielded a resolution of 20–30 nm in x-y and 50–60 nm in z directions.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization precision data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The 3D-STORM yielded a resolution of 20–30 nm in x-y and 50–60 nm in z directions.
source: The standard deviations of the distribution of these localizations were 9 nm in lateral and 22 nm in axial dimensions, and the corresponding full width at half maximum (FWHM) values were 22 nm and 52 nm, respectively (Figure 3b), which yielded a resolution of 20–30 nm in x-y and 50–60 nm in z directions.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization precision data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Two clusters of localizations separated by 95 nm in the z axis were well resolved.
source: Figure 3c shows an example of two clusters of localizations separated by 95 nm in the z axis being well resolved according to the z profile.
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution demonstration data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Fluorescent beads were used as fiducial markers to correct for sample drift.
source: We used fluorescent beads as fiducial markers to correct for sample drift as previously described (Rust et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim describes a method used in the study and is supported by citation.

claim: The distributions of localizations from Alexa-647 fluorophores were less spread out after stage drift correction.
source: Figure 3d shows the distributions of 492 localizations from 23 Alexa-647 fluorophores were less spread out after stage drift correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by drift correction data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Specific fine-scale nanostructures of MB-labeled target DNA were consistently obtained in different EGFP cell nuclei.
source: In different EGFP cell nuclei (outlined in red in Figure 4a, top row), we consistently obtained specific fine-scale nanostructures (Figure 4a, row D) of MB-labeled target DNA, shown as the detailed morphologies in the zoomed views (Figure 4a, row E).
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The identified nanostructures were composed of 100–1800 localizations.
source: These images were composed of 100–1800 localizations, which is comparable to the number of localizations (100–400) collected from the Oligopaint-labelled 4.9 kb sequences (Beliveau et al., 2015) and sufficient for delineating fine-scale 3D structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization counts from STORM images and comparison with prior work.

claim: The number of localizations (100–1800) is comparable to the number collected from Oligopaint-labelled 4.9 kb sequences (100–400) and sufficient for delineating fine-scale 3D structures.
source: These images were composed of 100–1800 localizations, which is comparable to the number of localizations (100–400) collected from the Oligopaint-labelled 4.9 kb sequences (Beliveau et al., 2015) and sufficient for delineating fine-scale 3D structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior work and assessment of localization numbers.

claim: The MB-FISH method was able to resolve sub-structures separated by a lateral distance of 41 nm or structural features of 35–43 nm in size.
source: As shown in Figure 4c, the corresponding FWHMs along cross-sections defined by the red line in Figure 4a showed our method was able to resolve sub-structures separated by a lateral distance of 41 nm or structural features of 35–43 nm in size (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by FWHM analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Nanostructures were detected in 21 out of 78 EGFP cells but zero in 83 blank cells (hypergeometric p value=5.0 × 10−8).
source: Collectively, we detected nanostructures in 21 out of 78 EGFP cells across multiple independent experiments, but zero in the 83 blank cells (hypergeometric p value=5.0 × 10−8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of detection rates across experiments.

claim: The detection of nanostructures in EGFP cells but not blank cells demonstrates the capability and specificity of the MB-FISH imaging method.
source: Collectively, we detected nanostructures in 21 out of 78 EGFP cells across multiple independent experiments, but zero in the 83 blank cells (hypergeometric p value=5.0 × 10−8). These findings demonstrate the capability and specificity of our MB-FISH imaging method.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the detection rate data.

claim: A 2.5 kb super-enhancer at −45 kb upstream within the Nanog locus in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) was chosen as a secondary target for super-resolution visualization.
source: As a secondary target for super-resolution visualization, we chose a 2.5 kb super-enhancer at −45 kb upstream within the Nanog locus in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) (Blinka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and is supported by citation.

claim: 34 MB probes were designed for the Nanog enhancer target: 24 MBs for minus strand and 10 MBs for plus strand.
source: Avoiding repeats that appear in other genomic regions, we designed 34 MB probes according to the target sequence: 24 MBs for minus strand and 10 MBs for plus strand (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim describes the probe design for the Nanog enhancer experiment.

claim: The Nanog enhancer MBs had dramatically reduced background fluorescence (15.8 ± 5.9%) in FISH hybridization buffer in the presence of NCSs, compared to the fluorescence readings in the presence of the CS.
source: The spectrophotometry analysis revealed that these MBs had dramatically reduced background fluorescence (15.8 ± 5.9%) in FISH hybridization buffer in the presence of NCSs, compared to the fluorescence readings in the presence of the CS (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectrophotometry data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout was used to generate homozygous knockout (HoKO) cells in which a 3 kb region covering the super-enhancer target was deleted from both alleles.
source: To obtain a cell without this super-enhancer as the negative control, we applied CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout in CJ9 mESCs (Shen et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2015) to generate homozygous knockout (HoKO) cells, in which a 3 kb region covering the super-enhancer target was deleted from both alleles.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design for generating negative control cells.

claim: The knockout of the Nanog enhancer was confirmed by PCR and sequencing.
source: The knockout was confirmed by PCR (Figure 5c) and sequencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: MB-labeled structures were detected in 14 of the 92 WT cells, but none in any of the 74 HoKO cells (hypergeometric p value=1.6 × 10−4).
source: We detected MB-labeled structure(s) in 14 of the 92 WT cells, but none in any of the 74 HoKO cells (hypergeometric p value=1.6 × 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of detection rates in WT vs HoKO cells.

claim: The detection of structures in WT cells but not HoKO cells demonstrated the specificity and robustness of the MB-FISH imaging method.
source: We detected MB-labeled structure(s) in 14 of the 92 WT cells, but none in any of the 74 HoKO cells (hypergeometric p value=1.6 × 10−4). These results demonstrated the specificity and robustness of our MB-FISH imaging method.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the detection rate data.

claim: The identified nanostructures of the Nanog enhancer were composed of 150–1200 localizations.
source: The identified structures were composed of 150–1200 localizations (numbers in the bottom row in Figure 5d), comparable to numbers observed in the integrated viral DNA imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization counts shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The MB-FISH method was able to resolve sub-structures separated by a lateral distance of 59 nm and structural features of 25–46 nm in size for the Nanog enhancer.
source: The corresponding FWHMs along cross-sections (indicated by a red line in Figure 5d) demonstrated the ability of our method to resolve sub-structures separated by a lateral distance of 59 nm and intriguing structural features of 25–46 nm in size (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by FWHM analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The combination of MB-FISH and 3D-STORM imaging allows super-resolution visualization of 2.5 kb unique genomic elements in situ in the nuclear genome.
source: Taken together, the combination of MB-FISH and 3D-STORM imaging allows super-resolution visualization of 2.5 kb unique genomic elements in situ in the nuclear genome.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the results from both viral DNA and Nanog enhancer experiments.

claim: The MB-FISH method directly visualized 2.5 kb non-repetitive DNA sequence in situ in human or mouse genome, which is the shortest unique genomic sequence resolved to date at super-resolution.
source: We demonstrated our MB-FISH method could directly visualize 2.5 kb non-repetitive DNA sequence in situ in human or mouse genome, which is the shortest unique genomic sequence resolved to date at super-resolution.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion claim based on the experimental results.

claim: Similar to the Oligopaint-labeling method, a set of MB probes can be bioinformatically designed to label a known unique genomic locus on either target strand, avoid repetitive sequences, and can provide allele specificity by probing sites covering single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
source: Similar to the Oligopaint-labeling method (Beliveau et al., 2012; Boyle et al., 2011; Beliveau et al., 2015; Yamada et al., 2011), a set of MB probes can be bioinformatically designed to label a known unique genomic locus on either target strand, avoid repetitive sequences, and can provide allele specificity by probing sites covering single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from maternal or parental chromosome.
evidence: This claim compares MB-FISH capabilities with Oligopaint methods and includes citations.

claim: MB-FISH could be combined with other super-resolution techniques, such as STED, if these techniques can image fluorescent dyes at a density of a few tens of molecules in 2.5 kb genomic DNA.
source: In the future, we expect our MB-FISH could be combined with other super-resolution techniques, such as STED (Donnert et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2016), only if these techniques must be able to image fluorescent dyes at a density of a few tens of molecules in 2.5 kb genomic DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications with citations to STED methods.

claim: Any reported dye used in STORM imaging with an available corresponding quencher could be applicable for MB probes, such as Atto-488, Atto-565, Alexa-647, or Cy5.
source: In regard to suitable fluorophores for MB probes, any reported dye used in STORM imaging with an available corresponding quencher could be applicable, such as Atto-488, Atto-565, Alexa-647, or Cy5 (Dempsey et al., 2011; Heilemann et al., 2009, 2008; Lehmann et al., 2015; Rust et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim discusses potential fluorophores for MB-FISH and is supported by citations.

claim: It might be possible to label and image three genomic elements using sets of MBs carrying Atto-488, Atto-565, or Alexa-647, respectively, using multi-color STORM to detect interactions among loci in situ in single cells.
source: It might be possible to label and image three genomic elements using sets of MBs carrying Atto-488, Atto-565, or Alexa-647, respectively, as well as using multi-color STORM to detect interactions among loci in situ in single cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential multi-color applications.

claim: MB-FISH differs from Oligopaint-FISH in that MB-FISH appeals to imaging condition optimization to achieve sufficient localization density, whereas Oligopaint-FISH depends on a secondary probe.
source: First, to achieve sufficient localization density, Oligopaint-FISH depends on a secondary probe, whereas MB-FISH appeals to imaging condition optimization.
evidence: This claim compares the two methods based on the experimental approaches described.

claim: Oligopaint-FISH applies a relatively high temperature for hybridization (37°C, 42°C or 47°C) to address non-specific fluorescence noise, whereas MB probes dramatically quench fluorescence from unbound or non-specifically bound probes.
source: Second, both methods involve high concentrations of fluorophore-conjugated probes (0.71 µM in MB-FISH vs >1 µM in Oligopaint-FISH), which unavoidably leads to interference from non-specific fluorescence noise. To address this issue, Oligopaint-FISH applies a relatively high temperature for hybridization (37°C, 42°C or 47°C), whereas MB probes dramatically quenches fluorescence from unbound or non-specifically bound probes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim compares the two methods and is supported by data in Figure 1d.

claim: The hybridization temperature used by MB-FISH (22°C) was lower than that used by Oligopaint-FISH (up to 47°C).
source: Third, the hybridization temperature used by MB-FISH (22°C) was lower than that used by Oligopaint-FISH (up to 47°C) and chosen based on optimal MB-CS binding, chromatin accessibility as well as simplifying the FISH steps (performed at laboratory temperature).
evidence: This claim compares hybridization temperatures between the two methods.

claim: The low hybridization temperature reduces background fluorescence and promotes probe-target binding, hence decreasing the number of input probes needed for STORM imaging (as few as 29 probes for MB-FISH vs ~106 probes for Oligopaint-FISH).
source: The low hybridization temperature reduces background fluorescence (Figure 1e) and promotes probe-target binding, hence decreasing the number of input probes needed for the STORM imaging (as few as 29 probes for MB-FISH vs ~106 probes for Oligopaint-FISH).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature-dependent binding data in Figure 1e and comparison with Oligopaint methods.

claim: Oligopaint-FISH has a sequence resolution of 4.9 kb, but MB-FISH managed to improve the resolution down to 2.5 kb.
source: Fourth, Oligopaint-FISH has a sequence resolution of 4.9 kb, but MB-FISH managed to improve the resolution down to 2.5 kb due to the need of fewer input probes and the lowered melting temperature for the hybridizing region.
evidence: This claim compares the sequence resolution capabilities of the two methods.

claim: The hybridizing region of Oligopaint was of a length of 32 to 42 nt, whereas MB adopted a hybridizing region length of 42 nt to ensure the probe hairpin structure would break upon associating with target sequence.
source: Fifth, the hybridizing region of Oligopaint was of a length of 32 to 42 nt, whereas MB adopted a hybridizing region length of 42 nt to ensure the probe hairpin structure would break upon associating with target sequence.
evidence: This claim compares the probe design between the two methods.

claim: The proximal distance between an Alexa-647 and a BHQ3 from two neighboring MBs will be 24 nt (10 nt plus the length of two flanking 7-nt arms), which is about 7–8 nm and largely avoids inter-molecular quenching.
source: Thus, the proximal distance between an Alexa-647 and a BHQ3 from two neighboring MBs will be 24 nt (10 nt plus the length of two flanking 7-nt arms), which is about 7–8 nm and largely avoids inter-molecular quenching (Wu and Brand, 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from probe design and is supported by citation on quenching.

claim: MB-FISH is suitable for shorter elements such as enhancers or promoters, whereas Oligopaint-FISH works well in large chromosome domains.
source: In this regard, MB-FISH is suitable for shorter elements such as enhancers or promoters, whereas Oligopaint-FISH works well in large chromosome domains (Beliveau et al., 2015; Boettiger et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim compares the optimal applications of the two methods and includes citations.

claim: MB-FISH could be a complementary approach to other existing methods, including Oligopaint-FISH, for visualizing a non-repetitive genomic sequence.
